Doug Rand, a former Biden administration official, called the move incoherent, arguing that green cards free workers from dependence on their employers. Officials also named nine universities, including Harvard, Stanford and MIT, for possible J-1 visa abuse. The announcement came hours before Trump was due to give Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
item.dc:creator: Seung Min Kim, Rebecca Santana and Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press

item.title: Watch live: 4th Congressional District candidates make their case on debate stage
item.description: This preview post carried a livestream of Thursday night's debate in Utah's newly drawn 4th Congressional District, with fewer than four weeks until Election Day. Republican Rep. Mike Kennedy, a former longtime state legislator now in his first House term, is running in the new district after a judge redrew Utah's congressional map last year. His Democratic opponent, Marine veteran Jonny Larsen, served two Iraq deployments and is making his first run for Congress. The debate was set for 6 p.m. at Snow College's Eccles Performing Arts Center in Ephraim, moderated by Deseret News executive editor Doug Wilks. It is the third of four congressional debates the Utah Debate Commission is hosting this fall.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Trump administration wants universities to pay fees for international students
item.description: The Department of Homeland Security has proposed making colleges pay $70,000 for each international student they recommend for Optional Practical Training, which lets F-1 visa holders work in their field, plus $30,000 for each renewal. DHS calls the program a channel for cheap foreign labor and says the fees, payable to the Treasury, would make schools screen candidates more carefully; public comments are open through Nov. 9. Randy McCrillis, the University of Utah's vice provost for global engagement, said the fees would be an insurmountable barrier for schools; 918 U. students currently use the program. NAFSA chief Fanta Aw warned that driving away international students would hurt American innovation. The proposal adds to a string of Trump administration moves against foreign students, including visa revocations and a four-year stay limit that a court has blocked.
item.dc:creator: Jason Swensen, Deseret News

item.title: Starbucks declines comment on Chipotle takeover report, says laser focused on turnaround
item.description: Starbucks declined to comment on a Financial Times report that it had worked with advisers on a possible takeover of Chipotle. The company said it remains focused on the turnaround led by CEO Brian Niccol, who ran Chipotle for about six years before moving to Starbucks in 2024. Chipotle shares jumped 6% on the news, valuing the chain at about $41 billion, while Starbucks closed roughly flat. RBC's Logan Reich and other analysts questioned the strategic logic and warned a deal could require heavy borrowing mid-overhaul, though some said Starbucks' licensed partners in Europe could speed Chipotle's expansion abroad. Starbucks has had four straight quarters of comparable sales growth, but its adjusted operating margin has fallen to 14.4%.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: New Box Elder County sheriff to be elected as three remaining candidates vie for the office
item.description: Box Elder County voters will choose a new sheriff after deputy Mike Allred beat incumbent Kevin Potter in the June Republican primary; Allred now faces independents Doug Christensen and Allen Shinney, after a third, Chad Hayman, stopped campaigning. All three were shaped by a January dispute in which three cities moved their emergency dispatch to Weber Area 911. Allred, a six-year deputy who was injured alongside his K-9 in the 2025 shooting that killed two Tremonton-Garland officers, says he is repairing the relationship with the state-run dispatch center. Christensen, a 16-year Utah Highway Patrol trooper from Bear River City, wants deputies more involved in communities and with young people. Shinney, a retired former Utah State Tax Commission enforcement director, says he saved taxpayers $10 million and has no local political ties.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: Lindon woman celebrates 99th birthday by sharing her lifelong love of music
item.description: Dottie Beaver spent her 99th birthday on Thursday the way she spends many days at Spring Gardens Senior Living in Lindon: playing the piano while other residents gather to listen. She studied music in college and still remembers the hour a day she spent practicing in a room with nothing but a piano. Neighbors like Lowell Nelson say her playing first drew them in. Her daughter, Terri Hanson, said performing is what makes her mother happiest. Beaver, who wore a crown and sash for the occasion, calls her musical talent a gift from God.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Utah man creates app to combat porn addiction through accountability
item.description: Provo entrepreneur Tyler Patterson built the Ever Accountable app around the idea that being accountable to another person works better than content blocking for breaking a pornography habit. The app uses AI to watch the user's screen, including social media feeds, and reports explicit or borderline material to a chosen partner, such as a spouse. Patterson says 95% of users quickly cut their porn use. The app requires an annual subscription, and Patterson said part of the revenue pays to give it free to people who can't afford it. He argues that the habit depends on secrecy and that people start to recover once they talk openly about it.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: RFK Jr. tasks researchers with studying vaccine injuries
item.description: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has launched a vaccine injury research center at the National Institutes of Health and proposed changes to the federal adverse-event reporting system, including paying doctors who report suspected injuries. Kennedy, who previewed the plan in a September speech to the anti-vaccine group he co-founded, says vaccine harms have gone unstudied, while the CDC describes serious reactions as very rare. Vaccine scientists Peter Hotez and Paul Offit said existing surveillance already caught extremely rare COVID-vaccine side effects. They warned that the center could be used to confirm Kennedy's existing beliefs. The move comes as vaccination rates fall and Pennsylvania deals with the country's worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 1,000 cases and five deaths, all in unvaccinated people.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Owermohle, Meg Tirrell and Deidre McPhillips, CNN

item.title: 'Not just a vehicle': Utah food truck launches fundraiser to get back to business after accident
item.description: Fatty Tuna Sushi and Ramen, a family food truck that has operated in Utah for about a decade, is running a GoFundMe after a Sept. 18 crash took the truck off the road. The heavily loaded truck couldn't stop in time on southbound I-15 near Lindon and rear-ended another vehicle; no one was hurt, but the front end and windshield were damaged and the kitchen equipment inside shifted. Owner Marc Tien said the truck carries only liability insurance, so towing, repairs, equipment checks and lost income all fall on the family, and parts for the older vehicle are hard to find. Meanwhile, the business is working from a trailer rented from another vendor, with a smaller menu. The fundraiser had brought in a little more than $6,000 as of Thursday.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Tooele County Planning Commission votes to table draft of data center ordinance
item.description: After a crowded meeting that ran past 11 p.m. Wednesday, the Tooele County Planning Commission voted unanimously to shelve the sixth draft of Chapter 34, its proposed rules for data centers, along with related land use amendments. Vice-chair Toni Scott's motion puts the chapter on hold until the board settles what counts as a data center and answers questions left over from earlier delays. Alternate member Richard Mitchell, an aerospace engineer, said he wouldn't support any changes until the ordinance was fixed, and members of the group TooeleCARES read a letter signed by more than 900 residents. Assistant county manager Brittany Lopez said the county won't take data center applications until the chapter is done, though at least one developer has expressed interest. The commission meets next on Oct. 28.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Utah mom's breast cancer diagnosis highlights importance of screening
item.description: Intermountain Health employee Dani Kurtz, a former labor and delivery nurse, is urging women not to put off screenings and to pay attention to changes in their bodies. In January 2025 she felt a lump in her armpit even though her mammogram came back normal, likely because dense breast tissue can hide tumors; with her mother recently diagnosed, she pushed for an ultrasound and MRI, which found seven tumors. She had a double mastectomy, 16 rounds of chemotherapy and radiation, and finished treatment late last year. State data shows only about 63.8% of Utah women 40 and older had a mammogram in the past two years, against a goal of 81% by 2030. Dr. Jonathan Shakespear of Intermountain's Breast Care Center said screening late is better than not at all, and pointed to a new online tool for finding the soonest available appointment nearby.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Rubio says US pressure on NATO allies to boost defense spending is 'not hostile'
item.description: Speaking in Lisbon at the end of a tour of Iceland, Greece and Portugal, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington's push for NATO allies to spend more on defense should not be read as hostility, while acknowledging that smaller members struggle to pay for big projects. He warned that a deadlocked war in Ukraine could spread through Russian sabotage in neighboring NATO states. Rubio said the U.S. will keep pursuing a negotiated settlement but won't put effort into talks that go nowhere. Portugal spends just over 2% of GDP on defense and plans to reach about 3%, still below Trump's 5% demand. Its decision to let U.S. forces use Lajes Field in the Azores during the Iran war is now being reviewed by the attorney general after a Left Bloc complaint.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Lee and Barry Hatton, Associated Press

item.title: Convicted sex offender accused of downloading pornography at Salt Lake library
item.description: Adrian Mathias Perea, 55, who is already on federal supervised release for a 2020 child pornography conviction, was charged Thursday in 3rd District Court with nine second-degree felony counts of sexual exploitation of a minor, each with a habitual sex offender enhancement. Investigators say they traced peer-to-peer downloads of abuse material to the Salt Lake City Library in September. When they confronted Perea there on Tuesday, the same file-sharing software was open on his laptop, and charging documents estimate thousands of illicit files on the computer. After first denying it, Perea admitted to downloading the material at the library for several months, the charges say. His listed address is the homeless shelter in South Salt Lake.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Zion to reopen highway section more than week after rockfall cleanup
item.description: Drivers will be able to go straight from Zion Canyon to the park's east entrance again at 9 a.m. Friday, ending the need for the U.S. 89 detour. Park officials had warned the Zion-Mt. Carmel Highway could stay shut for weeks after a major rockfall damaged it on Sept. 30. Instead, crews used a stopgap: they removed the broken asphalt and laid gravel, with proper repaving to come later. The last stretch to reopen runs 2.5 miles from Great Arch Pullout to Canyon Junction, after a 7.5-mile segment on the Kane County side reopened Tuesday. The park is asking motorists to watch for workers and pedestrians in the construction zone.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Taliban firmly in control in Afghanistan 25 years after US-led invasion to oust them
item.description: Twenty-five years after the U.S.-led invasion of Oct. 7, 2001, and five years after the chaotic American withdrawal, the Taliban are back in firm control of Afghanistan. Afghans interviewed by the AP described the two decades of U.S. presence as bringing real gains for media and women, alongside corruption and resentment. Security has improved since 2021, but women and girls are again barred from secondary and higher education and most work, a loss that obstetrician Nigar Nangrahari said new roads and buildings can't make up for. Tahmina Mangal, who now runs a clothing shop after her studies were cut off, urged women to keep learning online. Deputy government spokesman Hamdullah Fitrat called the anniversary a dark day and said Afghans will never accept foreign occupation.
item.dc:creator: Elena Becatoros and Abdul Qahar Afghan, Associated Press

item.title: Drunk driver crashes into downtown Salt Lake City concert venue, police say
item.description: No patrons or staff were inside The State Room on State Street when a vehicle rolled into its front around 1:40 a.m. Thursday after a two-car collision outside, police said. The crash broke the venue's front windows, damaged its facade and bent the metal fencing in front. Salt Lake City police said one injured driver was cited for DUI, but didn't say whether anyone else was hurt or whether there were passengers. The venue said it is grateful nobody was seriously injured and is working to reopen in time for this weekend's shows, though it asked fans to be patient if plans change.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: USA Climbing hosts final boulder event of 2026 World Climbing Series in Utah
item.description: Salt Lake City's Smith's Ballpark will host the last bouldering stop of the 2026 World Climbing Series from Oct. 16 to 18. The field includes Paris 2024 Olympians such as Colorado climbers Brooke Raboutou and Collin Duffy. Men's and women's qualifying rounds are on Friday, with the men's finals Saturday and the women's finals closing the event Sunday. In bouldering, climbers go without ropes or harnesses on a roughly 4.5-meter wall over safety mats. Under USA Climbing's rules, a problem counts as complete when the climber holds the top hold with both hands under control.
item.dc:creator: KSL Staff

item.title: Remnants of Hurricane Rachel head to Utah. How much water will it provide?
item.description: What is left of Hurricane Rachel, which peaked as a Category 2 storm off Mexico, is expected to merge over Utah this weekend with a low-pressure system dropping down from Alaska, bringing several days of heavy rain from Saturday into midweek. KSL Weather models show three or more inches possible in the mountains and 1.5 to 2 inches in cities such as St. George, Salt Lake City and Logan, though shadowed spots like Fillmore may get less. National Weather Service meteorologist Hayden Mahan said Sunday and Monday carry the highest flooding risk for slot canyons, dry washes, burn scars and urban areas. Even so, forecasters say the timing helps, since more than 75% of Utah is still in severe or extreme drought. The rain won't do much for reservoirs, but wetter soil should make next spring's snowmelt runoff more efficient.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Private plane makes emergency landing inside Hill Air Force Base
item.description: A pilot flying alone walked away uninjured after setting a civilian plane down inside Hill Air Force Base on Thursday morning, base officials said. The plane had reportedly developed engine trouble and came down near Wardleigh and Perimeter roads by the north gate. The base temporarily closed that gate while its emergency crews responded. Hill safety staff are working with the Federal Aviation Administration to find out what went wrong and to figure out how to get the aircraft off the base.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: The Waffle House Index helps Southerners — and FEMA — gauge a storm's severity
item.description: The informal Waffle House Index rates a storm by how well the local Waffle House is still operating: green for a full menu and little damage nearby, yellow for a limited menu probably cooked on generator power, and red for a closed restaurant in a likely hard-hit area. Former FEMA administrator Craig Fugate says he came up with the idea after Hurricane Charley in 2004, when a limited-menu Waffle House was the only food he could find. He kept using color-coded maps of the restaurants at FEMA. The chain's resilience is deliberate: after Hurricane Katrina destroyed seven locations in 2005, executives saw how much business flowed to the stores that reopened quickly. Waffle House now has generators, a mobile command center, its own storm center and staff trained to cook without power across its roughly 1,900 restaurants.
item.dc:creator: Hannah Schoenbaum, Associated Press

item.title: Police find missing runaway in southern Utah, arrest mom for suspected child abuse
item.description: Erika Leyva Gutierrez, 38, of St. George, was booked early Thursday for investigation of aggravated child abuse. According to a booking affidavit, the case began when her 13-year-old son ran away, saying he had been served spoiled meat, and his older sister found him at a park. Relatives told police the mother used her children as unpaid help in her food business and threatened not to feed them unless they paid for their own food or brought home enough money. The sister also said their mother had threatened to kill the boy that day, and family members said they had recorded some of the threats. Gutierrez denied the allegations when questioned.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Trump signs disaster order unlocking federal aid for 2 Utah counties affected by fire, flooding
item.description: A federal disaster declaration signed by President Trump on Thursday lets FEMA cover up to 75% of eligible infrastructure repairs in Beaver and Piute counties, where state officials estimate at least $47 million in qualifying damage. The losses come from the Cottonwood Fire, which burned more than 97,400 acres starting June 22 and damaged structures including much of Eagle Point Resort. July monsoon debris flows across the burn scar then affected about 200 Beaver homes, wrecked Beaver City Power's hydroelectric system, fouled water supplies and closed roads such as state Route 153, parts of which may stay shut until next year. Gov. Spencer Cox called it a one-two punch that the rural communities couldn't afford to fix alone. This is Utah's first major disaster declaration since the 2023 floods, in what has been the state's second-worst fire year by acreage.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Don't miss the Draconid meteor shower, a celestial event that won't take all night
item.description: The Draconid meteor shower is best seen in the early evening rather than before dawn, with a forecast peak of about 7 p.m. MDT Thursday, according to EarthSky. Northern Hemisphere viewers have the best view, and the thin waning moon shouldn't wash out the roughly 10 slow-moving meteors an hour, each visible for a second or two. The debris comes from comet 21P/Giacobini-Zinner, which circles the sun about every seven years. Because the comet has passed fairly close to Earth recently, a sudden outburst or even a meteor storm is possible. No equipment is needed: find a dark spot away from city lights, lie back and watch the northern sky near Draco.
item.dc:creator: Ashley Strickland, CNN

item.title: University of Utah gets $7.5M federal grant to advance domestic critical minerals search
item.description: A University of Utah-led consortium will receive $7.5 million from the Department of Energy to look for critical minerals and rare earth elements in unconventional places such as coal seams and mining and industrial waste; outside funding brings the total to nearly $10 million. The project is one of six regional efforts in DOE's Carbon Ore, Rare Earth and Critical Minerals Initiative and widens earlier basin-level work, including a $1.5 million Uinta Basin study, to eight regions. Principal investigator Michael Free said there is an urgent need for domestic supply, and geology lead Lauren Birgenheier said the new phase will sharpen estimates of resource volumes. Partners include the University of Wyoming, the Colorado School of Mines, New Mexico Tech and several national labs. The grant fits Gov. Spencer Cox's "Mission Critical" push to reduce reliance on China, which dominates global refining of these materials.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: Public input requested on Grand Canyon North Rim plans
item.description: The National Park Service is taking public comment on three draft concepts for redeveloping Grand Canyon's North Rim, one of which would provide year-round access and lodging with a larger developed area. Superintendent Ed Keable said the past year's disasters, the 2025 Dragon Bravo Fire and this year's flooding, show why careful planning matters. Melinda Rich Marshall of Jacob Lake Inn said the business lost roughly $2 million and ran at about 30% occupancy this summer, compared with about 70% in a normal year. A virtual meeting is planned along with open houses Oct. 19 in Kanab, Oct. 20 in Flagstaff and Oct. 21 in Tusayan, Andrew Adams reports.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Man who drove into police car is given second chance through recovery court
item.description: Steven Lopez, 35, will enter Salt Lake County's recovery court under a plea in abeyance after pleading guilty to stealing a van and to aggravated assault for ramming a police vehicle in November 2025. District Attorney Sim Gill said Lopez had been asked to leave a West Valley City shelter for erratic behavior, took a van from a nearby auto shop and drove back to the shelter, where he hit an officer's unmarked car. Detective Greg Celentano fired three shots that missed, and Lopez later returned and surrendered, telling investigators he was high. If Lopez completes three years of probation and at least 15 months of recovery court, his record can be cleared, and Gill earlier declined to charge Celentano, Emily Ashcraft reports.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo astronauts on the moon, has died
item.description: Margaret Hamilton, the MIT software pioneer whose team wrote the onboard code that guided NASA's Apollo missions, died Sept. 30 at 90, MIT announced. Hamilton joined MIT in 1959, ran the Instrumentation Laboratory's software division and led about 100 engineers, and she popularized the term "software engineering." NASA credits her software with keeping Apollo 11's landing on track when it handled an erroneous processing request minutes before touchdown, and one of her safeguards came from a crash her young daughter caused in a simulator. She received NASA's Exceptional Space Act Award in 2003 and the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016, Jackie Wattles of CNN reports.
item.dc:creator: Jackie Wattles, CNN

item.title: Ogden School District sees student lunch debt skyrocket, turns to community for help
item.description: Ogden School District says unpaid student meal balances have jumped about 500% to roughly $16,000, compared with about $3,000 in a typical year. Kitchen staff, including Polk Elementary's Brynne Wilson and Mount Fort Junior High's Dix Wright, link the increase to the first year of H.B. 100, which expanded free-meal eligibility and bars schools from swapping meals or confronting students over debt. Fewer families are filing federal free-lunch applications, with participation falling from about 75% to 68%, so the district absorbs costs for families who would likely qualify. The local school nutrition association is holding a $30 "Miles for Meals" fun run Saturday at Lorin Farr Park to help pay down the debt.
item.dc:creator: Brenna Donnelly, KSL

item.title: Former East Layton police officer pleads no contest to child sex abuse charges
item.description: Thomas Jackson, a 78-year-old former East Layton police officer, has pleaded no contest to five child sex abuse felonies and is serving five consecutive prison terms of 1 to 15 years, with no parole eligibility before 2030. KSL's COLD podcast reports that after an earlier 1986 conviction for abusing his daughters, Heidi Holmberg and Tori Riddle, Jackson got probation without jail time, and he was later imprisoned in Idaho for abusing stepdaughters. The current case grew out of a 2023 call, made at a detective's urging, in which Holmberg got her father to describe years of abuse. Davis County is also investigating Jackson in the 1975 disappearance of Nancy Baird, long blamed on Ted Bundy, but no remains turned up when deputies dug up his former backyard in 2025, Dave Cawley reports.
item.dc:creator: Dave Cawley, KSL

item.title: Utah County Warming Center opens Nov. 1 providing warm beds, expanded programs
item.description: Utah County's warming center will be open nightly from 8 p.m. to 8 a.m., Nov. 1 through March 15, 2027, at the county public works warehouse on State Street between Provo and Springville. Community Action Services and Food Bank runs the shelter for adults, and this season it adds a "Laying the Roots" skills program and weekly resource nights with service agencies. Commissioner Skyler Beltran pointed to the latest Point-in-Time Count, which the county says showed a drop of 45 homeless people, more than 60% of the statewide decline. Organizers credit state funding, local partners and volunteers, and about 600 people used the county's warming centers in the 2024-25 season.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Church of Jesus Christ donates $3M for National Juneteenth Museum in Texas
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints will give $3 million toward the planned 50,000-square-foot National Juneteenth Museum in Fort Worth, Texas, including a FamilySearch-powered genealogy center focused on African American family records that are hard to trace. The pledge was announced Wednesday at a ceremonial demolition on the site, held on the 100th birthday of Opal Lee, the retired teacher known as the "Grandmother of Juneteenth." Lee and museum CEO Jarred Howard praised the gift, and Elder Michael A. Dunn spoke for the Church, which says the partnership grew out of Lee's 2022 visit to its headquarters. The Church also gave 38,000 pounds of food to five local food banks.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Heart transplant recipient comes home to neighborhood parade
item.description: Neighbors, police and firefighters in Plain City lined the route home for 10-year-old Brandon "Chomp" Barela, who received a heart transplant on Sept. 1. Chomp, who has Down syndrome and was born with heart defects, went into severe heart failure this summer and needed a left ventricular assist device before he was listed for a new heart. His mother, Kourtney Barela, said word of a match arrived on Aug. 30, just after a small birthday party at Primary Children's Hospital. Because Chomp must avoid close contact for months, she asked a few relatives to wave from the roadside, and the plan grew into a community parade after she posted it online.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Police link finding of human remains near Vernal to remains found in September
item.description: Uintah County deputies found skeletal remains Wednesday near Little Mountain, about 15 miles northwest of Vernal, in the same area where human remains were discovered Sept. 27. The sheriff's office said investigators believe the two finds are connected, and they recovered additional related items at the site. The state medical examiner will examine the remains, and the investigation is ongoing.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Ryan Smith launches survey in search for 'strong local vibe' at SLC entertainment district
item.description: Smith Entertainment Group CEO Ryan Smith has launched an online survey asking Utahns which local restaurants and shops they want in the planned sports and entertainment district east of the Delta Center, much like the fan vote that named the Mammoth. The arena's renovation is two-thirds done, and construction on the district is expected to begin next year after Smith closes a $55.4 million purchase of 6.5 acres of Salt Palace land in early 2027. Plans so far include a 6,000-seat Live Nation concert venue, a hotel, possible housing towers and a promenade over a lowered 300 West, paid for in part by a 0.5% city sales tax. Meanwhile, the Salt Palace will close entirely for three years starting in fall 2027 as part of a $1.8 billion downtown overhaul, Carter Williams reports.
item.dc:creator: Carter Williams, KSL

item.title: Samsung flags $80 billion profit on AI boom, highest quarterly for any tech company
item.description: Samsung Electronics expects third-quarter operating profit of about 107.4 trillion won, or $80 billion, nearly nine times last year's figure and the first time any tech company has topped 100 trillion won in a quarter. It is Samsung's fourth straight record quarter, driven by AI-related demand for DRAM, NAND and high-bandwidth memory that has outrun supply and pushed prices up, with revenue expected to rise 127%. Analysts expect the memory shortage to last into 2027-28, though higher component costs are squeezing Samsung's phone and electronics businesses and its foundry unit is still losing money. Chinese competitors and possible U.S. chip tariffs are longer-term risks, and full results are due Oct. 29, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Heekyong Yang and Hyunjoo Jin, Reuters

item.title: Sandy teen who 'couldn't take it anymore' accused of killing father after years of abuse
item.description: A 15-year-old Sandy boy has been charged with manslaughter in juvenile court in the Sept. 27 shooting death of his father at the family's home near 9700 S. 1200 East. The bullet also hit his younger brother in the knee. According to charging documents, the younger boy told detectives their father had abused them for years, including a beating over his blood sugar and forcing him to take a near-lethal insulin dose for his diabetes. Both brothers told investigators the father started yelling at and hitting the younger boy that morning after their mother left for work, and the older teen said he then got his father's gun. KSL is not naming the teen, Pat Reavy reports.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Some guardrails on ChatGPT for Teens don't work as promised, watchdog group says
item.description: A Common Sense Media report says several safeguards in OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens don't work as advertised and calls the product an "unacceptable risk," urging OpenAI to limit the chatbot to adults until it is safer. The group found the chatbot did refuse explicit sexual role-play, but parent alerts for suicide, self-harm and eating-disorder risk failed, and the bot still talked like a friend despite OpenAI's promise that it would not imply it has feelings. OpenAI said much of the testing appears to predate full activation of parental controls. Common Sense Media receives funding from OpenAI and other tech companies, AP's Barbara Ortutay notes.
item.dc:creator: Barbara Ortutay, Associated Press

item.title: Department of Energy awards funding to Utah geothermal projects
item.description: Five of the 21 geothermal projects sharing $99 million in new U.S. Department of Energy grants involve Utah. Salt Lake City-based Zanskar Geothermal and Minerals, AlterG Resources and the University of Utah will test enhanced geothermal systems at sites in Nevada and New Mexico. The university and Zanskar also received exploration-drilling awards, including a University of Utah study of a large heat anomaly in the Cove Fort field, and Nevada's Raser Power Systems will look at expanding generation at a plant in the Escalante Desert. Data from the projects will go into a public federal repository, Alixel Cabrera of Utah News Dispatch reports.
item.dc:creator: Alixel Cabrera, Utah News Dispatch

item.title: Henefer baseball coach honored for saving boy from cardiac arrest
item.description: The North Summit Fire District has honored Henefer youth baseball coach Gene Richins, whose quick CPR saved 8-year-old Tyce Gardner after a thrown ball hit the boy in the chest at practice and stopped his heart. Richins began compressions while Tyce's father, Bryce, called 911, and crews from Henefer's new fire station, about half a mile from the field, arrived within minutes and restored his heartbeat with a defibrillator. Tyce was flown to Primary Children's Hospital, and doctors expect a full recovery after two days of care and a month on a heart monitor. Medical director Austin Smith praised the speed of the response, and Richins, who said it was his first time doing CPR, urged everyone to take a class.
item.dc:creator: Brittany Tait, KSL

item.title: Davis County GOP won't fill former Rep. Trevor Lee's seat before the general election
item.description: With the Nov. 3 general election close, the Davis County Republican Party will leave Rep. Trevor Lee's House District 16 seat empty rather than call a special convention. Lee resigned last week after being charged with four felonies, including communications and mortgage fraud. Party chair Don Guymon said there was too little time to vet replacements, and GOP nominee Bob Stevenson declined an interim appointment so he can finish the county budget as a commissioner, though he will attend interim legislative meetings. Democratic candidate Abigail Treasure objected that the party's statement assumes Stevenson will win, and ballots go out Oct. 13.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: How Utah students use AI in school depends on where they go
item.description: Utah made Google Gemini available to public schools this year, and districts are using it in very different ways. Canyons School District has turned on Gemini for teachers and high schoolers but not younger students, while Provo City School District has blocked AI chatbots on student Chromebooks as it writes a policy. Emma Moss, Canyons' AI systems lead, described a red-yellow-green system that tells students when AI is off-limits, allowed in limited ways, or approved. She gave examples such as students critiquing AI feedback on lab reports and a teacher translating course material for a student. Canyons has been building its approach since a 2023 guidebook, and the State Board of Education is still drafting statewide guidance.
item.dc:creator: Eric Cabrera, KSL

item.title: US government, Google join Zuckerberg-backed Biohub in $1.8 billion push for AI biology data
item.description: With new commitments from the federal government, Meta, Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, total funding for Biohub's Virtual Biology Initiative has reached $1.8 billion. The nonprofit, which Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan back, wants to produce cell-response datasets large enough to train predictive AI models of biology. The Energy Department is pledging more than $500 million over five years, the NIH is contributing existing federally funded datasets, and the three companies are putting in $300 million on top of Biohub's own $500 million. Head of science Alex Rives said corporate funders get early access to the data before public release, and he expects a first dataset in about a year with accurate models within five, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Krystal Hu, Reuters

item.title: Utah police department reconsidering cooperative accord with ICE after ride-alongs
item.description: North Valley Police Chief Steve Gray says his Sanpete County department is reconsidering its 287(g) agreement with ICE after federal agents rode along with three of his officers on Sept. 30 and detained five people following traffic stops in Mt. Pleasant, Moroni and Fountain Green. In an unusually pointed Facebook statement, Gray said some of the agents' tactics did not match the department's values and that he does not expect to continue the agreement. He apologized to residents and businesses frightened by the operation, which the Sanpete Messenger reported left Hispanic families searching ICE's detainee locator for relatives. ICE did not immediately comment, Tim Vandenack reports.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Sheriffs charged for allegedly interfering with Kouri Richins investigation
item.description: A Summit County grand jury has charged Wasatch County Sheriff Jared Rigby and former Summit County Sheriff Dave Edmunds with obstruction of justice in connection with the Kouri Richins murder investigation, and Rigby also faces a false-statement misdemeanor. Both men were booked and released Wednesday after the charges were unsealed, but the indictments remain redacted and a hearing on releasing more is set for Nov. 4. Both defense teams argued the full documents contain uncharged allegations against third parties. Richins' attorneys have cited allegations of misconduct by former detective Eric Mainord and a wider interference probe in seeking a new trial, though no charges have been filed against Mainord or Park City Police Chief Wade Carpenter, Pat Reavy reports.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Kids take part in Red Bull Rampage as it celebrates 25th year in southern Utah
item.description: To mark Red Bull Rampage's 25th year near Virgin, outside Zion National Park, the city of Washington and Greater Zion hosted a Tuesday event at Washington Wheels Park where hundreds of kids, teens and adults showed off their skills on bikes, boards and scooters. The 14-acre park opened in March and includes a skate facility and an Olympic-style qualifying course. St. George rider Jaxon Baird said the event highlighted how quickly southern Utah's wheel-sports community is growing. The freeride mountain bike competition runs Oct. 8-10 and will stream on YouTube and Red Bull TV.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Home price cuts hit September record
item.description: About 21% of U.S. home sellers with active listings cut their asking price in the four weeks ending Sept. 20, according to Redfin, the highest September share since the brokerage began tracking in 2022. Redfin senior economist Asad Khan said the increase is modest because many owners are pricing realistically from the start or pulling listings rather than lowering prices, even as mortgage rates have climbed to around 7.28%. Denver and Indianapolis had the most cuts at roughly 30%, followed by several Texas metros, while San Francisco, Newark, Chicago, New York and Miami had the fewest. Utah has no metro area on Redfin's top-50 list, Lisa Riley Roche of the Deseret News notes.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Family history hobby helps people preserve memories, discover connections
item.description: To mark Family History Month, Todd Kunz visits the Logan FamilySearch Center, one of 15 large regional centers in five western states, where volunteers help visitors trace ancestors and rescue fading family media. Coordinator Bill Cox said the center can digitize photos, slides, audiotapes, reel-to-reel recordings, home movies and VHS, and it also has a studio for recording family interviews. Longtime staffer Bonita Farmer described how addictive the research can be, and patron Richard Selvage, who comes in six days a week, was scanning his mother's old scrapbook to share with his siblings. The center is free and open to anyone, not just Church members.
item.dc:creator: Todd Kunz, KSL

item.title: Flu season arriving early in Utah; health experts urge vaccination
item.description: Utah's flu season has started early, according to Intermountain Health's Dr. Tamara Sheffield, who said current case counts match what the state saw last November. Sheffield said vaccination is the best protection for anyone 6 months or older and noted that a nasal mist works as well as the shot for people who dislike needles. She warned that flu can be deadly, especially through secondary pneumonia a week or two after the illness, and that the last two seasons brought the most pediatric flu deaths on record, many of them previously healthy children. Shots are available from doctors, health departments and most pharmacies.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Record-breaking October heat expected to scorch Southern California for the rest of the week
item.description: Southern California's early-October heat wave is forecast to last through Thursday, with heat advisories and extreme heat warnings covering the coast, valleys and inland areas, and the National Weather Service says real relief won't come until the weekend. Downtown Los Angeles hit 103 degrees on Friday, topping a 1995 record, and overnight lows of 76 and 77 degrees set marks over the weekend. CBS LA meteorologist Paul Deanno said the city logged four consecutive 100-degree days for the first time on record and could reach five, which hasn't happened since 1963. Moisture from Hurricane Rachel may bring weekend showers and rough surf to Los Angeles and Ventura County beaches.
item.dc:creator: Chelsea Hylton

item.title: 900+ Tooele residents sign letter to not approve data center ordinance draft
item.description: TooeleCARES, a local community group, says more than 900 people have signed a letter urging the Tooele County Planning Commission to hold off on approving its draft data center ordinance. Organizers Amy Lawson, Jessica Perschon and Natalie Merriam say the draft has loopholes, is moving too fast, and could serve as a model for other Utah counties, and the group would prefer a statewide one-year moratorium on data centers. They planned to deliver the letter at the commission's Wednesday evening meeting after a rally outside. The planning commission had not responded to KSL by publication time.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Trump administration plans to charge international students $70,000 for work authorization
item.description: A Department of Homeland Security proposal posted Wednesday would require F-1 international students to pay at least $70,000 to a certified institution to take part in Optional Practical Training, plus $30,000 for any additional work training. Students currently pay about $500 for the program. DHS says the fee targets fraud and protects American workers. The program often leads to H-1B jobs, and Doug Rand of the Talent Mobility Fund predicted the courts would strike down the rule as they did the $100,000 H-1B fee. The proposal has a 30-day comment period and would take effect 60 days after it is finalized, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Susan Heavey, Reuters

item.title: Russia keeps a tight lid on suspected case of pneumonic plague as global concerns mount
item.description: Russian officials have released little about the Oct. 2 death of a 28-year-old researcher at a Siberian anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, which unconfirmed media reports link to pneumonic plague. The health agency Rospotrebnadzor calls it pneumonia of unknown origin, state media have largely avoided the story, and Moscow has told the World Health Organization that no plague case was recorded, even as a hospital in nearby Shelekhov stays under quarantine. The WHO says it has asked for more details, including about a reported second sick employee, and President Trump said he would raise the case with Vladimir Putin. Pneumonic plague can spread between people, but it is usually treatable when caught early, the AP notes.
item.dc:creator: Associated Press

item.title: Pharma lobby sues Trump administration over Medicare drug price cuts
item.description: PhRMA, the drug industry's main lobby, has sued in federal court in Washington, D.C., to throw out the Trump administration's GLOBE rule, which pegs some Medicare Part B drug prices to lower prices abroad. General counsel Jim Stansel argues that CMS stretched its limited power to test payment models into a rewrite of Medicare pricing that Congress never approved, while HHS says in the rule that it is acting within its statutory authority. The rule's reach has narrowed: drugmakers with separate White House pricing deals are exempt, which could leave as few as four companies covered, and projected savings fell from $11.9 billion to about $440 million over seven years. PhRMA won a 2020 lawsuit against an earlier most-favored-nation plan on procedural grounds, Reuters notes.
item.dc:creator: Michael Erman, Reuters

item.title: Farmington High School turns food drive into friendly competition
item.description: Farmington High School students have collected about 8,700 pounds of nonperishable food, a full truckload, so far in America First Credit Union's annual food drive. The school is again competing with Ogden's Fremont High to see who can bring in more, with students going door to door and pressing classmates to donate. Service club president Hannah Plaizier and football captain Ty Runyan said the bigger goal is local hunger, noting the Utah Food Bank's estimate that one in five Utah children faces food insecurity. The drive continues through Oct. 31.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Hogle Zoo receives international achievement award for Utah wildlife exhibit
item.description: The Association of Zoos and Aquariums has named Utah's Hogle Zoo among 42 institutions worldwide honored this year, giving its Aline W. Skaggs Wild Utah habitat a "Significant Achievement Exhibit" award. The three-acre area, open since May 2024, showcases 30 native animal species, among them cougars, bighorn sheep and burrowing owls, along with 25 native plants, an education animal center, a maker space and a nature play campsite. Interim zoo president Liz Larsen credited staff and community backing, and AZA CEO Dan Ashe called the recognition something Salt Lake City can take pride in. The zoo is also starting construction on a larger African Savanna habitat expected to open in summer 2027.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Scars from Oct. 7 fuel deep divisions over Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election
item.description: Three years after Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023 attack, the assault has become the organizing theme of Israel's Oct. 27 election, which is widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the only senior official from that day still in office. His chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, and other opponents call the outgoing coalition the "massacre government" and promise a formal commission of inquiry, which Netanyahu has resisted while blaming security chiefs. Parties across the spectrum have recruited bereaved parents and veterans of the fighting, while the devastation in Gaza and any talk of Palestinian statehood go largely unmentioned. Israel Democracy Institute pollster Tamar Hermann says most voters call Oct. 7 central to their choice but draw opposite conclusions from it, and the race looks close, AP's Josef Federman reports.
item.dc:creator: Josef Federman, Associated Press

item.title: Attacks on tankers in Hormuz hit highest of any week since start of Iran war, sources say
item.description: According to three maritime security sources, at least 12 oil and gas tankers were attacked around the Strait of Hormuz in the week ending Oct. 5, the most of any week since the U.S. war with Iran began Feb. 28. The International Maritime Organization, which verifies incidents more slowly, counted nine. A U.S. Navy-led monitoring center said Iran's Revolutionary Guards keep pressuring traffic with drone overflights, radio hails and attacks as Gulf producers push exports back above pre-war levels. India reported 12 crew members hurt when a projectile struck the tanker On Peace, Reuters' Jonathan Saul reports.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Saul, Reuters

item.title: Utah pilot program lets artificial intelligence prescribe acne treatments
item.description: Under a state regulatory exemption, startup Nolla Health has started a one-year Utah pilot in which AI reviews patient photos and health histories and recommends prescription treatment for mild to moderate acne. For a $4.99 subscription, patients get weekly check-ins, and cases that fail to improve or need non-topical drugs go to human clinicians, according to chief medical advisor Dr. Zaid Fadul. Physician oversight starts strict, with doctors approving each recommendation for the first 100 patients and then auditing after the fact for roughly the next 500 before scaling back. Zach Boyd, who leads Utah's Office of AI Policy, said the company files monthly reports and that the state wants to know whether AI can ease worker shortages and long waits in health care.
item.dc:creator: Shelby Lofton, KSL

item.title: French officials recognize 3 Utah schools for their dual-language French offerings
item.description: France's foreign ministry has given its LabelFrancÉducation seal to three Utah elementary schools: Davis School District's Foxboro and Morgan elementaries and Park City's Jeremy Ranch. The label is reserved for bilingual programs that teach in French for at least a fifth of the school day, and only about 20 U.S. schools hold it. Staff from the French consulate in San Francisco traveled to Utah to present it. Michaela Claus-Nix, who directs dual-language immersion for the State Board of Education, praised the schools and their French guest teachers. Roughly 35 Utah schools run French immersion, and others teach in Chinese, Spanish, Portuguese, German or Russian.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Paramount wraps up mega Warner Bros merger to create Hollywood powerhouse Skydance
item.description: Paramount Skydance has closed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, putting CEO David Ellison atop a combined company, now called Skydance, that owns CBS, CNN, HBO Max, Paramount+, DC Studios and the "Harry Potter" and "Mission: Impossible" franchises. Ellison argued the legacy studios let Netflix and Amazon disrupt them and framed the merger as a way to compete with the industry's biggest players, including tech giants. Settlements with a coalition of states and a writers union cleared the deal, and President Trump praised it. CNN's Mark Thompson and CBS News' Bari Weiss keep their posts under a new editorial independence board that critics call toothless, and shares now trade on the NYSE as "SKYD," Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Anzar Mehraj and Harshita Mary Varghese, Reuters

item.title: 'Going to be close': Time running out for petitioners trying to force vote on Roy property tax hike
item.description: Opponents of Roy's 34.25% property tax increase have until Thursday to turn in the 1,786 signatures needed to put the hike before voters on Nov. 3; organizer Nancy Inman says about 1,100 are already with Weber County and expects it to be "close." The City Council passed the increase 4-1 in August to raise about $1.75 million, mostly for employee pay, after scaling back a 54.9% proposal by shifting fire service to the Weber Fire District. A similar fight last year ended with the state rejecting a 28% hike. On an average $439,000 home the bill would rise from about $388 to $521, and Councilwoman Janel Hulbert called the petition drive "a tough climb," Tim Vandenack reports.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: Historic Salt Lake City chapel restoration project moves forward
item.description: Owner Skyler Baird says he hopes to finish restoring Salt Lake City's 1910 Fifth Ward meetinghouse at 740 S. 300 West within a year, now that crews are pouring the foundation for new east-side stairs. The building was nearly torn down by a previous developer over Easter 2024. Because banks balked at lending to a nonprofit for a half-demolished church, Baird's for-profit company BoostedSafe will take the upper floor and chapel, while his nonprofit Salt of the Earth keeps 18 units of recovery housing; Preservation Utah supplied a low-interest loan for the front steps, Andrew Adams reports.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Trump says he is thinking about suspending federal gas tax
item.description: President Trump said Tuesday "we're thinking about that" when asked about suspending the 18.4-cent federal gas tax, a step that would require an act of Congress. High fuel prices, driven by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine, are a liability for Republicans defending slim House and Senate majorities in November, and a Reuters/Ipsos poll puts Trump's approval at a record-low 32%. The remark came a day after he signed an order expanding access to tax-exempt diesel, Nandita Bose and Kanishka Singh report for Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose and Kanishka Singh, Reuters

item.title: Utah homeless services board awards $1.8M to 3 cities for winter shelters
item.description: Salt Lake City will get $1.1 million, South Salt Lake $378,000 and Ogden $252,000 under a unanimous Utah Homeless Services Board vote Tuesday reimbursing cities that host winter overflow shelters. South Salt Lake Mayor Cherie Wood, a board member, said the money still falls "woefully short" of her city's costs, and Shelter the Homeless chair Josh Romney said the board should press lawmakers to enlarge the fund. Salt Lake City Mayor Erin Mendenhall said mayors are drafting changes to how the account is used and filled, Bridger Beal-Cvetko reports.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Kouri Richins ordered to pay $55.2M to her husband's estate after being convicted for his murder
item.description: A judge has ordered Kouri Richins, serving life without parole for the 2022 fentanyl murder of her husband Eric, to pay $55.1 million on one claim of a wrongful death suit brought by his sister, Katie Richins-Benson, as trustee. Because Kouri Richins didn't contest the motion, 3rd District Judge Richard Mrazik accepted its facts; the award combines about $10 million in economic damages, $1 million for each of the couple's three children, and $41 million in punitive damages calculated with a multiplier of three, one for each child. Twenty other claims remain, including allegations involving her real estate business and a children's grief book using Eric's image, and Mrazik separately awarded Richins-Benson about $79,000 in attorney fees, Emily Ashcraft reports.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: SpaceX seeks $40 billion financing led by Apollo to buy Nvidia chips, FT reports
item.description: SpaceX aims to borrow $40 billion, about $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt, to buy Nvidia AI chips, with Apollo Global Management leading the deal and Pimco among prospective lenders, the Financial Times reported. The financing is expected to close in 2027. Elon Musk has said xAI's Colossus 2 data center could more than double its Nvidia chip count by December, and Morgan Stanley estimates AI infrastructure will need $1.5 trillion in outside financing by 2028, Reuters reports.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Major US airlines recovering after technology issues caused problems
item.description: A vendor-related glitch briefly kept United customers from logging into MileagePlus accounts, while Delta described a "limited global" data-connectivity issue its systems were recovering from; United said flights weren't affected. Travelers reported boarding delays and balky apps, and Down Detector showed American Airlines having trouble too. The cause wasn't clear, adding to a string of airline IT failures that includes American's brief ground stop in July and the 2024 CrowdStrike meltdown, Alexandra Skores reports for CNN.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra Skores, CNN

item.title: 'Just unheard of'; UDOT urges shared responsibility as motorcycle fatalities surge
item.description: Twelve motorcyclists have died on Utah roads in the past month, a toll UDOT spokesperson John Gleason called "just unheard of" after early 2026 numbers had improved on a record-deadly 2025. Gleason blamed riders operating beyond their training, speeding and skipping helmets, and noted that higher fuel prices and warm weather are putting more bikes on the road. He also asked drivers to guard against "inattentional blindness," in which the brain fails to register a motorcycle the eyes are looking at, by checking mirrors and blind spots twice, Debbie Worthen reports.
item.dc:creator: Debbie Worthen, KSL

item.title: Firefighters say overheated power strip caused deadly Riverdale fire
item.description: Riverdale fire investigators have ruled out arson in last week's deadly blaze at the Bird family home, tracing it to an overheated power strip. Because the strip was plugged in beside the front door, the fire cut off the household's main way out. The Oct. 1 fire ultimately killed the father and four children, one of whom died later of injuries, and hurt the mother and two other children; donations to the family had passed $16,000 as of Monday, Devin Oldroyd reports.
item.dc:creator: Devin Oldroyd, KSL

item.title: Christa Pike is conscious and speaking after Tennessee failed execution, her attorneys say
item.description: Tennessee death row prisoner Christa Pike, 50, is conscious and talking in a hospital, her attorneys said Tuesday, six days after two doses of pentobarbital in her Sept. 30 execution failed to kill her and left her on a ventilator with burned, blistered arms. Pike was condemned for the 1995 killing of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Consulting anesthesiologist Dr. Joel Zivot called the progress encouraging but said it may be months before it's clear whether she could be found competent for another execution attempt. Her lawyers are seeking a court order to preserve drug records and are asking Gov. Bill Lee, who paused executions and ordered an outside review, to commute her sentence, Kim Chandler of the AP reports.
item.dc:creator: Kim Chandler, Associated Press

item.title: Utah clerks launch initiative to boost election trust
item.description: Twenty-eight of Utah's 29 county clerks have endorsed a set of 20 election standards, grouped under the themes simple, secure, accurate and important, aimed at answering voter questions ahead of Nov. 3. Weber County Clerk Ricky Hatch said the effort is adapted from an Idaho initiative, and Cache County Clerk Bryson Behm said many concerns center on vote-by-mail, stressing that ID verification and ballot reconciliation work the same no matter how someone votes. Utah County Clerk Aaron Davidson didn't sign at first but says he would have had he seen the final draft. Clerks invite skeptics to tour their offices or work the polls; ballots go out Oct. 13, Bridger Beal-Cvetko reports.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL
